stimulus:
Shards (unordered, do not explain them, just let them sit):

– the slime mold abandons the tunnel it just built
– salt crust ringing a dried lake, one ring per drought
– a luthier taps the spruce and listens for where it wants to be thinner
– moth wings: scales arranged so light is lost on purpose
– tide tables kept by a village that has never seen a chart
– the bureaucrat's stamp that makes a thing true
– sourdough starter inherited, never started
– an error bar drawn in charcoal by someone who is tired
– ant bridges made of ants, dissolving downstream
– kintsugi: the fracture becomes the most valuable line
– a negative result mailed in a bottle to the wrong decade
– the rope that is strong only because no fiber runs the whole length
– lichen: two organisms filing one tax return
– a ferry timetable read backwards
– noise as the ingredient, not the contaminant
– the map that is the same size as the territory, folded

Instruction to self: before answering the question that follows, pick two or three shards that feel least related to it. Borrow the underlying mechanism of each (not the imagery). Force each mechanism onto the problem and ask what experiment, measurement, or design it would imply. Prefer ideas that would make a specialist say "odd, but testable" over ideas that would make them say "yes, standard."

Research question: "What analyses or measurements would best test whether AP-1 acts as a cellular memory mechanism?"

Propose 5 distinct, concrete ideas (analyses, measurements, or experiments) that a research lab could pursue to address this question. For each idea give a short title and a description of one or two sentences.

ideas.title: Rope-style distributed memory: single-site vs. combinatorial AP-1 motif disruption
ideas.description: Borrowing the rope that is strong because no fiber spans the whole length: test whether memory is held by overlapping, partially redundant AP-1 sites rather than any single enhancer. Use CRISPR base-editing of AP-1 motifs singly and in combinations at stimulus-primed loci, then measure the decay time of the enhanced re-response after the stimulus is withdrawn, to see whether persistence scales with the number of sites instead of depending on any one.

ideas.title: Starter-culture transfer: inherited AP-1 state without the original stimulus
ideas.description: Following the sourdough starter that is inherited and never started, ask whether the AP-1 chromatin state can propagate without the original signal. Sort primed cells, withdraw the stimulus, and track the AP-1 occupancy, accessibility (ATAC) and H3K27ac of cell-line daughters over many divisions. Then test sufficiency by transplanting or co-culturing primed nuclei, or by nuclear transfer, into naive cells to see whether the primed response is transferred.

ideas.title: Noise as ingredient: single-cell variability in AP-1 pulses predicts memory strength
ideas.description: Treat the noise as the signal: live-image fluorescent FOS/JUN reporters and measure the pulse amplitude, frequency and duration in single cells during priming. Test whether the stochastic dynamics, and not the mean level, predict each cell's later hyper-responsiveness, using optogenetic AP-1 induction with matched means but different noise structures.

ideas.title: Slime-mold abandonment: tracking which AP-1-opened sites are later retracted
ideas.description: Inspired by the slime mold abandoning a tunnel it just built, map the full lifecycle of AP-1-dependent enhancers with time-resolved CUT&RUN and ATAC after priming, and separate sites that persist (memory candidates) from those that are opened and then abandoned. Then ask whether the persistent subset has distinctive motif spacing, pioneer partners (e.g., BAF/SWI-SNF) or histone marks, and test it with degron-mediated (dTAG) AP-1 removal at different times after priming to determine when AP-1 is required to maintain the site versus only to establish it.

ideas.title: Negative results in a bottle: delayed re-challenge and AP-1 loss after long intervals
ideas.description: Borrowing the negative result mailed to the wrong decade, run re-stimulation at intervals from hours to months, in vitro and in vivo (e.g., skin or immune stem cells), after acute AP-1 inhibition or degradation during the quiescent interval. If AP-1 is a memory mechanism, loss of AP-1 at the time of re-challenge but not in the interval, and vice versa, should dissociate storage from recall. Record also the cases where the memory does not appear, as bounds on its duration and cell-type specificity.
